Later I went to the terrace and let my hands shake for a minute. That was fine too.

Tuesday, 11 pm
Today was the meeting where I had to tell the team the launch is slipping by three weeks. My fault, partly. Two minutes before, my heart was hammering and every muscle said leave. Fake a call, go to the washroom, anything. I actually stood up. Then I stopped at the door and did the thing the counsellor taught me last year: feel both shoes on the carpet, breathe out slower than in, name three things. Grey chairs, a coffee ring on the table, Mahima's red notebook. I sat back down. My voice shook for the first sentence, and then it didn't. Mahima nodded at me halfway through, which helped more than she knows. Nobody shouted. The fear was still there the whole time, humming. But I was the one talking, not the fear. Proud of me tonight. Vijay

Dear Ramesh Mama,
You asked how exam prep is going, so here's the honest version. My shoulders are tight all day, like someone is pressing them down. At night my legs won't keep still, and my mind plays the same film: I fail maths, Papa goes silent, everyone at the wedding asks my marks. I know it's only a film. It still feels real at two in the morning.
This week I tried what you suggested. I made a timetable with a break every hour. When the film starts, I breathe out slowly and tell myself, 'That's a what-if, not a fact.' Last night I slept by eleven. Studying actually went better today. I'm still nervous. But I'm less scared of being nervous.
Thank you for asking properly.
Love,
Reena

Ward note, night shift
At 1 am Pema, our newest nurse, came out of bed 12 after a difficult conversation with a frightened family. I saw her go into the pantry and followed to check on her. She didn't reach for her phone, which I have seen her do before when upset, scrolling until break ended. Instead she stood with both feet planted, one hand on the counter, and breathed out slowly. Then, quietly, she named what she saw: 'Steel kettle. Blue mugs. Rain on the window.' After two minutes her colour came back. She told me that last month she had started seeing a counsellor, who taught her this. 'Scrolling made me feel nothing,' she said. 'This makes me feel here.' She finished her shift. I've suggested the whole team learn the steps at Friday's meeting.
Chinmay, ward in-charge

It happened on the metro again. Doors closed, the carriage packed, and my heart went off like an alarm. Old me would have got off at the next station, gone home and cancelled on Akash. I've cancelled on him three times this month. Today I tried the steps instead. Felt my feet in my sneakers, pressing down. Breathed out slowly, longer than in. I still felt shaky when I met Akash, but I was there. We ate momos and laughed. I'm writing this so I remember it works. And if this keeps ruling my days, I'll book the counsellor Akash mentioned. Disha

passage: Aadhya, come, sit. You think your Sarita Nani was never scared? When I was ten, in our village, I was sitting in the temple courtyard shelling peanuts. Nothing was wrong. Then suddenly my heart went thud-thud-thud like a drum at a wedding, the courtyard spun, and I was sure I was going to die right there among the peanut shells. I screamed for my Amma. When I was sixteen, in the crowded Friday bazaar, my heart suddenly pounded, my hands went numb, and I was sure I'd faint in front of everyone. It passed, but after that I was afraid of the fear.
